title: The skill vs custom tool decision rule (most of your "tools" should be skills)
description:
You reach for a custom tool when your agent needs a new capability. You write the code, wire the schema, deploy it. It feels like the serious answer.

But a tool is a server you own. Shipping it takes a deploy. Changing one line takes another deploy. And your agent can only call that tool from outside. It can never read what's inside it. A skill is the opposite: a markdown file the agent reads top to bottom and follows. Edit a line, save, and it ships in the same pull request as your prompt.

The decision rule I use: reach for a tool only when the model can't be trusted to improvise the work. Charging a card, running a migration, signing a release. That's deterministic execution you don't hand to the model, and it earns real code. Everything else (a workflow, a format, a checklist, an API recipe) is instructions, and instructions belong in a file the model just reads.

Honest limit: a skill is only as reliable as the model following it. For anything that must happen exactly, every time, the determinism of a tool wins. A skill can be skipped; a tool can't.

So next capability you add, ask one question: does the model need to be stopped from improvising this? If no, write the skill. Most of what you build into an agent isn't a tool. It's a skill you haven't written yet.
